messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For most of her life, Meena had organized herself around work, routine, and family. A 66-year-old South Asian woman, widowed for several years, she had kept going by taking shifts at a retail store, speaking warmly with regular customers, folding clothes, and straightening displays with the steady competence of someone used to carrying a household on her own. The assault happened after an evening shift. She had stayed later than usual to help close and was alone with a man when the store had largely emptied out. In recalling it now, Meena does not tell it as a smooth story. What comes are images, fixed and terrible, “like photographs,” as she describes them: a close view of his face, the angle of a back room door, the fluorescent light above her, the look of clothing half fallen from a rack. Some parts are painfully sharp, and she can state them with an exactness that startles her. Other stretches are simply absent. She knows time passed, but there are blanks she cannot fill. The memory returns to her as a series of snapshots rather than a full sequence, with a few moments preserved in perfect clarity and the rest missing.

What has stayed with her is not only the attack itself but the sense of violation in it. Meena had always believed there were lines decent people did not cross, especially with a woman alone, especially an older widow working to support herself. Since the rape, what catches her attention in daily life is not just danger in the usual sense, but misconduct, disrespect, people acting without conscience. At work, if she sees a customer shouting at a cashier, cutting in line, or speaking crudely, her body goes tight before she can think. She finds herself staring, heart pounding, with the same conviction rising in her: people can do terrible things and get away with them. The smell of smoke is another jolt. If someone passes the entrance after a cigarette break, or if there is a faint burnt smell from overheated wiring or something singed in the stockroom, she is abruptly back with those visual fragments, as if one of the photographs in her mind has been dropped in front of her again. The smell does not bring a full narrative, just those bright, frozen pieces.

Being alone with men has become especially difficult. If a male coworker steps into an aisle while she is restocking and there is no one else around, Meena feels trapped and exposed. She starts calculating where the nearest customer is, whether the front counter can see her, whether she should leave the cart and walk away. She does not tell herself that every man will assault her, but being alone with one feels intolerable in a way she cannot dismiss. Over the months, she has adjusted her work around this. She avoids going into the stockroom if a male employee is back there, asks to stay near the register where others are visible, and tries to swap tasks so she is not closing with men. These changes have narrowed her world at the store. Coworkers sometimes read her as difficult or particular, and Meena feels ashamed of that, though the alternative feels impossible.

Outside work, her life has become thinner. She says nothing feels meaningful anymore. After her husband died, she had still felt there was purpose in getting up, earning money, visiting relatives, cooking, managing. Since the rape, those same activities feel emptied out. She goes through them because they have to be done, not because they matter. Small frustrations now overwhelm her in ways that frighten her. A delayed bus, a mix-up in the schedule, a customer returning an item angrily—she feels as if even the slightest upset is more than she can handle. This loss of confidence has been humiliating for her. She used to think of herself as someone who endured hardship quietly. Now she worries she is no longer able to cope with ordinary life.

Running through all of this is her conviction that what happened was profoundly unjust. She returns again and again to the fact that she did nothing to invite it, that she was simply at work, doing what she had always done, and that there has been no real answer for what was done to her. The unfairness of that sits heavily with her. It sharpens her reaction when she sees other people behaving badly, because each instance seems to confirm the same ugly truth about how easily people violate boundaries and move on.

By the time Meena came for help, the strain had become visible even to others. She had started turning down shifts that might leave her alone with male staff, and her manager had asked whether she wanted to cut back her hours. A niece had noticed that Meena no longer wanted to go out and that she seemed flattened, as if nothing reached her. In session, Meena speaks quietly but with great intensity when those clear images arrive. What brought her in was not one dramatic crisis so much as the dawning realization that her life had shrunk around these moments and that she could no longer trust herself to manage even small disturbances. What frightens her most is the idea that this is how the rest of her life will remain—empty, unfair, and organized around avoiding what might happen when she is alone with a man or caught by one more smell, one more scene of people acting without decency. What she hopes for, carefully stated, is not to forget, but to be able to live without every upsetting moment turning her back toward those pictures.
